evidence.supporting_text: Consultation paper dated May 02, 2025 seeking comments/views/suggestions from the public and stakeholders on proposals for rationalizing the Placement Document for Qualified Institutions Placement (QIP).
evidence.extraction_note: All fifteen physical pages reviewed; merged comparison cells on pages 6–9 visually checked.

evidence.supporting_text: QIP is a key fundraising mechanism for listed companies; funds raised via QIP over FY2019-20 to FY2023-24 are tabulated (from 14 issues/INR 54,389 crore in 2019-20 to 61 issues/INR 68,972 crore in 2023-24), with QIP garnering 35% of total equity fund mobilisation by listed entities in 2023-24. SEBI recently reviewed and streamlined the rights-issue disclosure framework (reducing letter-of-offer disclosures, expediting timelines) given listed companies' existing comprehensive LODR periodic disclosures; since QIP issuers are similarly listed, the paper proposes reviewing Schedule VII (QIP disclosures) on the same basis to reduce duplication with information already public.
evidence.extraction_note: All fifteen physical pages reviewed; merged comparison cells on pages 6–9 visually checked.

evidence.supporting_text: Regulation 2(tt) of SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018 defines Qualified Institutions Placement as an issue of eligible securities by a listed issuer to qualified institutional buyers on a private-placement basis (including promoter/promoter-group offers for sale). Chapter VI of the ICDR Regulations lays down QIP's regulatory provisions: conditions for making a QIP, lead-manager appointment, placement document, pricing, application and allotment.
evidence.extraction_note: All fifteen physical pages reviewed; merged comparison cells on pages 6–9 visually checked.

evidence.supporting_text: Schedule VII of the ICDR Regulations currently mandates comprehensive QIP placement-document disclosures (risk factors, use of proceeds, financial information, industry/business description, organizational structure, taxation, auditors, etc.), which is time-consuming to prepare and may duplicate information already public under LODR continuous-disclosure obligations. QIBs are sophisticated investors who do not need the same disclosure depth as retail investors in a public offering. Preferential-issue disclosures (also private placements) are comparatively brief, and the recently rationalized rights-issue letter of offer likewise reduced disclosure content. On this basis, SEBI proposes reviewing Schedule VII to contain only relevant issue/issuer information.
evidence.extraction_note: All fifteen physical pages reviewed; merged comparison cells on pages 6–9 visually checked.

evidence.supporting_text: Proposes to rationalise the placement-document content by prescribing only relevant issue information (full revised content at Annexure-I). Existing-vs-revised comparison table begins: (1) Disclaimer - no change; (2) Glossary of terms/abbreviations - revised into four defined categories (conventional/general terms, issue-related terms, issuer/industry-related terms, abbreviations) to align with Schedule VI (IPO and Rights Issue); (3) Lead manager(s)/advisors - no change; (4) Summary of issue/eligible security - no change; (5) Risk factors - revised to require risks specifically in relation to the issue/object of issue and risks material to the issuer/business (with past-occurrence instances and impact where applicable), rather than generic industry/business risks that may not be relevant to investors.
evidence.extraction_note: All fifteen physical pages reviewed; merged comparison cells on pages 6–9 visually checked.

evidence.supporting_text: (6) Market prices - no change; (7) 'Use of proceeds' renamed 'Object of Issue' (same substantive content: purpose, cost break-up, financing means, deployment status) to align with Schedule VI terminology; (8) Capitalization statement expanded into a defined 'Capitalisation Statement' (total borrowings/equity/ratios, pre- and post-issue, based on the latest CFS) plus a new 'Capital Structure' sub-section (authorised/issued/subscribed capital, paid-up capital before/after issue and after conversion of convertibles) - currently undefined and often over-inclusive with unnecessary historical equity-raising detail; (9) Dividends in the preceding three years - no change.
evidence.extraction_note: All fifteen physical pages reviewed; merged comparison cells on pages 6–9 visually checked.

evidence.supporting_text: Existing rows 10-11 (three years' audited consolidated/unconsolidated financial statements plus latest reviewed financials, with full balance sheets, income statements, cash-flow statements, accounting-policy statements etc.) are consolidated and reduced to a defined extract of the latest financial year's audited consolidated financial statements (with comparative prior year) and latest limited-review financials, listing ten specific line items (total income, net profit before/after tax, equity share capital, reserves and surplus, net worth, basic/diluted EPS, return on net worth, NAV per share) with a reference to full audited reports already filed with stock exchanges, to avoid duplicating information; a note allows additional detail for QIPs marketed to foreign investors to satisfy international-law requirements, though this is not mandated by Schedule VII itself.
evidence.extraction_note: All fifteen physical pages reviewed; merged comparison cells on pages 6–9 visually checked.

evidence.supporting_text: (12) Management's discussion and analysis of financial condition and results of operations - proposed to be deleted entirely, as it is not required in rights issues or preferential issues; (13-14) Industry description and Business description - merged into a brief summary of the issuer's primary business and industry, since investors are already aware of such details; (15) Organizational structure - no change; (16) Board of directors and senior management - reduced from full biographical/office-tenure detail to name, date of birth, age, DIN, address, occupation and term-expiration date, to align with Schedule VI; (17) Latest shareholding pattern as submitted to stock exchanges - no change; (18) Taxation aspects - no change.
evidence.extraction_note: All fifteen physical pages reviewed; merged comparison cells on pages 6–9 visually checked.

evidence.supporting_text: Legal-proceedings disclosure (row 19), currently governed by the issuer's own LODR materiality policy, is restructured into: (I) outstanding litigations/legal proceedings likely to materially and adversely affect operations/financial position, summarised in tabular format with quantifiable amounts; and (II) specifically enumerated pending matters (criminal liability, material statutory violations, economic offences with initiated proceedings). Materiality is to be assessed as the LOWER of the issuer's own board-defined materiality policy, or specific value-based thresholds mirroring Schedule VI (2% of turnover, 2% of net worth (unless negative), or 5% of the average of the last three years' absolute profit/loss after tax) - aligning QIP litigation-disclosure materiality with the IPO/Rights Issue framework.
evidence.extraction_note: All fifteen physical pages reviewed; merged comparison cells on pages 6–9 visually checked.

evidence.supporting_text: (20) Auditors, (21) General information, (22) catch-all material-information clause, and (23) wilful-defaulter/fraudulent-borrower disclosures - all unchanged. Public comments on the proposals are invited, to be submitted not later than May 23, 2025 via SEBI's online public-comments form; technical issues in submission may be raised by email to consultationcfd@sebi.gov.in.
evidence.quote: The comments / suggestions along with rationale should be submitted not later than May 23, 2025
evidence.extraction_note: All fifteen physical pages reviewed; merged comparison cells on pages 6–9 visually checked.

evidence.supporting_text: Full text of the proposed revised Schedule VII (Annexure-I): (1) Disclaimer clause for QIP under Chapter VI ICDR Regulations; (2) Glossary categories; (3) Lead manager(s)/advisors; (4) Summary of issue/eligible security; (5) Risk factors (issue/object-of-issue risks and issuer/business-material risks, with historical occurrence/impact where applicable); (6) Market prices (high/low/average prices over three years, monthly high/low for six months, trading volumes, board-resolution-date price, six-month pre-filing volume); (7) Object of Issue (purpose, cost break-up, financing means, deployment status); (8) Capitalisation Statement and Capital Structure (as detailed in E006); (9) Dividends in the preceding three years.
evidence.extraction_note: All fifteen physical pages reviewed; merged comparison cells on pages 6–9 visually checked.

evidence.supporting_text: (10) Financial Information extract (ten line items as detailed in E007); (11) Primary business of the issuer and industry, in summary form; (12) Organizational structure; (13) Director/manager details (name, DOB, age, DIN, address, occupation, term-expiration date); (14) Latest shareholding pattern; (15) Taxation aspects; (16) Outstanding litigations and legal proceedings, with the materiality-threshold framework detailed in E009; (17) Statutory auditor's name, address, telephone and email; (18) General information; (19) Catch-all material-information clause; (20) Wilful-defaulter/fraudulent-borrower disclosures (name of person, declaring bank, year declared, outstanding amount, remedial steps, other disclosures).
evidence.extraction_note: All fifteen physical pages reviewed; merged comparison cells on pages 6–9 visually checked.

evidence.supporting_text: SEBI circular SEBI/HO/MIRSD/ MIRSD-PoD-1/P/CIR/2025/004 dated January 08, 2025, addressed to all registered Research Analysts and BSE Limited as RAASB, titled Guidelines for Research Analysts.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.supporting_text: SEBI states that the Research Analysts (Third Amendment) Regulations, 2024 were notified and came into force on December 16, 2024, and directs RAs to comply with those amendments and the guidelines under the amended RA Regulations.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.locator: Clause i — Qualification and certification requirements
evidence.supporting_text: Revised qualification requirements are not required for specified existing RA cohorts, while NISM certification and other Regulation 7(3) conditions continue to apply.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.locator: Clause ii(a)-(e) — Deposit requirement and table
evidence.supporting_text: Deposit amounts are set by maximum client count in the previous financial year: up to 150—₹1 lakh; 151-300—₹2 lakh; 301-1,000—₹5 lakhs; 1,001 and above—₹10 lakhs. The deposit is held with a scheduled bank under lien in favour of RAASB; existing RAs must comply by April 30, 2025, while new applicants are subject from the circular date.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.locator: Clause iii — Registration both as Investment Adviser and Research Analyst
evidence.supporting_text: An individual or partnership IA may be registered as an RA subject to separate compliance with each regime and an undertaking to maintain an arms-length relationship and segregate IA and RA services.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.locator: Clause iv — Registration as part-time research analyst and illustrations
evidence.supporting_text: The circular defines permissible and impermissible outside activities for part-time RAs, requires equivalent qualifications, arms-length segregation, a prominent non-SEBI-services disclaimer, conflict disclosure, and specified NOC/registration outcomes illustrated for professionals and other activities. Regulation 16A of the Intermediaries Regulations is reproduced as a condition.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.locator: Clause v — Designation as principal officer
evidence.supporting_text: A partnership RA with no partner meeting the minimum qualification and certification requirements must apply for RA registration as an LLP or body corporate by September 30, 2025.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.locator: Clause vi — Independent professional as Compliance Officer
evidence.supporting_text: A non-individual RA may appoint an eligible independent professional as compliance officer if prescribed NISM certifications are held; the principal officer must undertake responsibility for monitoring compliance. The circular lists the relevant NISM examinations.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.locator: Clause vii — Use of Artificial Intelligence tools in RA services
evidence.supporting_text: An RA or research entity using AI tools is solely responsible for client-data security, confidentiality and integrity, research-service outputs and legal compliance, and must disclose the extent of AI use in client terms; existing clients must be brought into compliance by April 30, 2025.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.supporting_text: Research services must be corroborated by a research report containing relevant data and analysis and the report must be retained. Research services supplied to a client who pays for another intermediary service are clarified to be for consideration even if no direct research fee is charged.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.locator: Clause ix — Fees chargeable to clients
evidence.supporting_text: The circular sets a ₹1,51,000 annual family cap for individual/HUF clients, excludes statutory charges, carves out non-individual/accredited/institutional proxy-adviser clients, restricts advance fees to one quarter, requires proportionate refunds without breakage fees, and sets transitional timing for existing and new clients. RAASB revises the limit every three years using Cost Inflation Index after consulting SEBI.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.locator: Clause x(a)-(f) and footnotes — Client-level segregation
evidence.supporting_text: Research and distribution services must be segregated at RA group/family and client level; clients choose one service within the group/family, PAN is the control record, existing holdings need not be liquidated, and family definitions are tied to specified RA Regulations provisions.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.supporting_text: Dependent family-member declarations, annual professional/auditor certification, a standard-waiver carve-out for exclusive institutional/accredited clients, exclusion of stock broking from distribution, and a June 30, 2025 compliance date are specified.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.supporting_text: Model-portfolio recommendations are treated as research services subject to SEBI guidelines in Annexure-A; RAs providing model portfolios must comply by June 30, 2025 and audit coverage extends to these obligations.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.locator: Clause xii — Disclosure of terms and conditions
evidence.supporting_text: RAs must disclose terms and conditions, obtain client consent before rendering research services or charging fees, include minimum mandatory terms in Annexure-B and MITC, and obtain existing-client compliance by June 30, 2025.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.locator: Clause xiii — KYC requirements and maintenance of record
evidence.supporting_text: RAs must perform KYC for fee-paying clients and retain interaction records for all clients including prospective clients from first interaction through completion, using legally verifiable forms.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.supporting_text: Interaction records must be maintained for five years, longer for disputes or SEBI preservation directions; KYC/record compliance is due by June 30, 2025. The circular also requires an annual RA compliance audit whose report specifies the provisions audited.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.supporting_text: Annual audit must be completed within six months after financial-year end; the report goes to RAASB/SEBI within one month, adverse findings and actions within one month and no later than October 31, segregation certification forms part of the audit, and audit status/adverse findings are published. Additional requirements start with FY ending March 31, 2025.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.supporting_text: An RA or research entity must maintain a functional website containing specified details and confirm website details and compliance to RAASB by June 30, 2025.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.locator: Paragraphs 3-5 — Applicability, enabling power and website location
evidence.supporting_text: The circular states that its provisions take effect on the date of the circular unless a clause says otherwise, cites section 11(1) of the SEBI Act read with the RA Regulations as authority, and states that it is available under SEBI Legal/Circulars.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.locator: Annexure-A, paragraph 1 and start of paragraph 2
evidence.supporting_text: Annexure-A defines a model portfolio as a weighted basket supported by a research report and defines required disclosures, launch date and update date; it begins the mandatory model-portfolio framework.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.supporting_text: A model-portfolio report must cover constituents, factsheet, methodology, labelling, investment horizon and predefined review/update frequency, and communicate rebalancing rationale.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.locator: Annexure-A, paragraph 2(vi)-(viii); Annexure-B heading and opening
evidence.supporting_text: Model-portfolio reports must disclose risk, use validated and appropriate benchmarking consistently, and fall within audit requirements. Annexure-B then makes minimum client terms and prior consent mandatory.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.supporting_text: Mandatory client terms cover election of research services, applicable SEBI law, client information and KYC, standard consent language, and RA registration/qualification declarations.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.locator: Annexure-B, continuation of clause 4 and clauses 5-8
evidence.supporting_text: Annexure-B requires RA declarations, fee-payment terms, risk and conflict disclosures, and disclosure of termination/refund arrangements following suspension or cancellation of RA registration.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.supporting_text: If RA registration is suspended for more than 60 days or cancelled, fees are refunded pro rata for the affected period. Client grievances must be resolved within seven business working days or another SEBI-specified timeline; disputes may use arbitration or other SEBI-specified mechanisms.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.supporting_text: Changes to voluntary additional clauses require 15 days notice; clients must be directed to the Do’s and Don’ts in SEBI master circular SEBI/HO/MIRSD-POD-1/P/CIR/2024/49 dated May 21, 2024; MITC must be disclosed and standardized with SEBI/RAASB consultation. MITC is standardised by ISF in consultation with SEBI and RAASB.
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.locator: Annexure-B, end of clause 12 and clause 13
evidence.supporting_text: MITC must state that an RA cannot execute trades for the client, and RAs must guide clients on the optional Centralised Fee Collection Mechanism for IA and RA (CeFCoM).
evidence.extraction_note: Complete source text reviewed; deposit table on physical page 2 also visually checked in this revision.

evidence.extraction_note: Rendered page checked against parsed text; the rendered reference number contains no extra space. The SEBI masthead is bilingual, but the substantive circular text is English.

evidence.supporting_text: SEBI states that the IA Second Amendment Regulations, 2024 were notified and came into force on December 16, 2024, and directs IAs to comply with those amendments and the following guidelines under the amended IA Regulations, 2013.
Regulation 8 deposit amounts are specified by maximum clients on any day of the previous financial year: up to 150 clients ₹1 lakh; 151-300 ₹2 lakh; 301-1,000 ₹5 lakhs; 1,001 and above ₹10 lakhs.
evidence.extraction_note: Deposit table visually inspected on rendered page 2.

evidence.supporting_text: The deposit is to be held with a scheduled bank under lien in favour of IAASB; applicable changes are revised by April 30 of the subsequent financial year; existing IAs must comply by June 30, 2025 and new IA applicants from the date of the circular.

An individual or partnership RA may be considered for IA registration if it separately complies with IA and RA regulatory/reporting requirements and gives an undertaking to maintain an arms-length relationship and segregate advisory and research services.

Part-time IA eligibility is defined by unrelated permitted work; equivalent IA qualifications/certifications, segregation, a minimum 10-font disclaimer for other services, disclosure of other activities and conflict avoidance are required; eligible professional examples are conditioned by Intermediaries Regulation 16A prohibitions.

Persons advising on assets such as gold, real estate or cryptocurrency are not eligible as part-time IAs; a CA giving incidental securities asset-class advice for tax planning need not register, but security-specific advice to a specific client requires part-time IA registration.
A partnership IA with no partner meeting the minimum qualification and certification requirements must apply for registration as an LLP or body corporate by September 30, 2025.

A non-individual IA may appoint an independent professional compliance officer subject to professional-body membership and specified NISM certifications; the principal officer must undertake responsibility for monitoring compliance to IAASB/SEBI.
evidence.extraction_note: Rendered pages 5-6 checked; certification list comprises NISM X-A, X-B, X-C and III-A.

evidence.supporting_text: IA Regulations cover investment advice related to securities under SEBI; for non-SEBI products/services in financial planning, IAs must disclose non-SEBI status and lack of SEBI grievance recourse and obtain a client declaration/undertaking at new-client onboarding, with existing clients compliant by April 30, 2025.

IAs using AI are solely responsible for client-data security, confidentiality and integrity, information used, AI-output-based advice and legal compliance; they must disclose the extent of AI use at agreement and as additionally required, with existing clients compliant by April 30, 2025.

The source states the AUA fee cap at 2.5% per annum per family, identifies the earlier fixed-fee limit as ₹1,25,000, revises the fixed-fee maximum to ₹1,51,000, and requires IAASB to revise and announce the limit once in three years using CII after consultation with SEBI.

The source states the earlier 12-month restriction on changing fee mode and now permits mode changes at any time; the maximum charge remains bounded by the higher of the fixed-fee limit or 2.5% of AUA, excluding statutory charges.

Fee limits apply only to individual and HUF clients, not non-individual clients or accredited investors, whose terms are bilaterally negotiated; fee limits apply only to advice concerning securities under SEBI, with AUA defined by the net asset value of such securities.

Existing Individual/HUF clients keep their current fee limit and fee mode until expiry of the current agreement or June 30, 2025, whichever is earlier; new clients are subject to the fee provisions from the circular date.

Clause ix(a) uses the wording “in-principal registration” while clause ix(c) uses “in-principle registration”; the same clause states that an individual IA crossing 300 clients at any time or ₹3 crore fees in a financial year, whichever occurs earlier, must enter the non-individual registration route.

In-principle non-individual registration is valid for up to three months to complete transition, after which the individual certificate is surrendered for final registration; existing clients may continue to be serviced during transition, and failure to obtain non-individual registration requires continuing within individual IA limits.

IAs serving exclusively institutional clients and accredited investors may avoid advisory/distribution segregation if the client signs a standard waiver; stock broking is not distribution for Regulation 22.

IA-client agreements must include standardised MITC, including that the IA cannot execute a trade without specific positive client consent for each trade; agreements must guide clients on optional CeFCoM and may be consented to by legally acceptable modes including DigiLocker Aadhaar e-sign. Clause xi(a) assigns ISF standardisation in consultation with IAASB and SEBI.
evidence.extraction_note: The MITC text was visually checked on rendered page 10.

evidence.supporting_text: For existing clients, IAs must disclose the specified agreement terms and obtain consent by June 30, 2025.
IAs providing implementation/execution services must record every telephone consent and timestamp such communications to preserve an audit trail, with compliance by June 30, 2025.
Regulation 19(3) requires an annual IA compliance audit, and the audit report must identify each IA Regulation, circular and guideline provision on which compliance is reported.

evidence.supporting_text: Annual audit must be completed within six months after financial-year end; the report is submitted within one month of its date; adverse findings and approved action are submitted within one month and no later than October 31 each year; an annual segregation certificate is obtained within six months after year-end and forms part of the audit.

IAs must publish audit-report status and adverse findings/action on their website, provide the audit report to clients, and apply the additional audit requirements starting with the audit report for the financial year ending March 31, 2025.
Regulation 19A requires an IA to maintain a functional website with specified details, and IAs must confirm website details to IAASB by June 30, 2025.

legal_effects.description: Establishes a single, comprehensive Cybersecurity and Cyber Resilience Framework (CSCRF) for SEBI Regulated Entities, structured into four Parts (Objectives and Standards; Guidelines; Compliance Formats; Annexures and References) and graded across five RE-category tiers.

This framework supersedes 21 pre-existing SEBI cybersecurity circulars/guidelines (Table 1, R001-R021) and 22 cybersecurity-related letters/advisories to named MIIs/AMFI (Table 2, R022-R043), per the two-tier implementation glide path (January 1, 2025 for six categories with a pre-existing circular; April 1, 2025 for other REs).

operative_change.summary: Annual categorisation and highest-category rule.
operative_change.new_or_proposed_position: Set the CSCRF category at the start of the financial year using the previous year’s data, retain it throughout that year and have it validated at compliance submission. Apply the highest category where multiple registrations exist. For CSCRF, the MII category includes KRAs and QRTAs. AIF AUM/VCF aggregate corpus thresholds are self below ₹100 crore, small ₹100–<500 crore, mid ₹500–<1,000 crore and qualified at least ₹1,000 crore. Brokers with up to 10,000 active UCC clients are self only without IBT/algo; with IBT/algo they are small; above 10,000–50,000 small, above 50,000–500,000 mid, above 500,000 qualified; QSB categorisation also applies. Custodian AUC is small below ₹1 lakh crore, mid ₹1–<10 lakh crore and qualified at least ₹10 lakh crore. Institutional DPs are qualified, other DPs mid; DDPs take the higher DP/custodian category. CIS, CRAs and non-excluded DTs are self; non-individual IAs small. Merchant bankers in conglomerate/systemically important groups are qualified, issue-management and the stated public-transaction activities mid, others small; listed merchant bankers also intimate exchanges. MF/AMC AUM is small below ₹10,000 crore, mid ₹10,000–<1 lakh crore, qualified at least ₹1 lakh crore. PMS is self below ₹1,000 crore, small ₹1,000–<3,000 crore, mid at least ₹3,000 crore. RTA folios are small 10,000–<1 crore, mid 1–<2 crore and QRTAs MII. Do not infer a QRTA threshold not stated here.

operative_change.summary: Identity, privilege, authentication and access logs.
operative_change.new_or_proposed_position: Maintain identity lifecycle, purpose/time/need-to-know access, least privilege, segregation, maker-checker, unique logs and physical/logical access policies; rank alone gives no access right. Revoke leavers/dormant/excess rights, lock failed logins and use MFA for untrusted access to trusted critical systems. Retain access logs at least two years, with six months online and the balance archived. Review access and privileged activity quarterly for MIIs/qualified and half-yearly for others. MII/qualified zero-trust and unused/delegated-token reviews are quarterly. Non-small/self requirements add privileged access management, password and internet controls, no alteration of own logs, network segmentation, web/email/DNS controls and allow-listing. All apply password complexity and deletion of unused generic IDs; more detailed password lifecycle/hash controls have the narrower applicability stated.

operative_change.summary: Data protection, nonproduction separation and source-code assurance.
operative_change.new_or_proposed_position: Protect data at rest/transit, classify it, maintain availability and leak controls, separate production and nonproduction and preserve integrity. Non-small/self guidelines require encryption including cloud in-use controls and full-disk/file encryption where possible. Customer-app security and real-time capacity planning apply except self. All protect backups/PII, avoid sensitive client-side HTML/cookie storage, renew certificates and use migration-integrity SOPs. MIIs/qualified REs separate environments and tests, address OWASP/SANS weaknesses and obtain critical source code or equivalent escrow including patches, vulnerability SLAs, vendor assessment and support. DevSecOps remains recommended. Annex H/I measures are illustrative except valid TLS expressly required for Internet pages with sensitive information; preserve equivalent-control audit requirements.

operative_change.summary: Secure development, configuration, change and release testing.
operative_change.new_or_proposed_position: Maintain approved baselines, secure development, change control, malicious-code scans, vendor certificates where source is not owned and security/functionality tests. All apply hardening, remove default accounts/services, restrict ports and scripting and use host firewalls where possible. Non-small/self guidelines require app allow-listing, regression before change, business-logic/security/load/recovery testing, vulnerability assessment at production releases and VAPT for major releases. A major release includes the specified regulatory, core software, login, interface, protocol, market and process/schema changes. Critical software receives DAST/SAST, cyber-functional/API and integrity audits, SOC logs, configuration audit, SBOM and a requirements matrix. New-technology maturity and threat-modelling examples remain guidance where labelled.

operative_change.summary: Maintenance, remote working and severity-based patching.
operative_change.new_or_proposed_position: Approve/log maintenance and remote access, assess vendor/remote risks and use severity-based OEM patches tested in an equivalent nonproduction environment before PDC/DR. Non-small/self remote-work controls include trusted devices, MAC/IP and host integrity and continuous alerts. Replace critical end-of-life/end-of-support systems; legacy virtual patching requires documented legitimate constraints and lasts at most six months. MIIs/qualified REs maintain an annually approved patch policy and quarterly compliance reports, test post-patch capacity and patch PDC/DR high severity within one week, moderate within two weeks and low within one month; emergencies follow the OEM clock.

The 23 weighted metrics cover budget, vulnerability mitigation, staff training, remote MFA, SIEM assets, change control, contingency testing, privileged access, incident reporting, maintenance, media, physical entry, agreements, screening, risk assessment, procurement contracts, mobile encryption, risk management, critical asset identification, CSK closure, policy, SOC efficacy and automation. Weights total 100. Budget 10%, critical-assets share 50% and CSK 15-day targets are scoring inputs, not independently created duties/deadlines. Rating bands are 91–100 exceptional, 81–90 optimal, 71–80 manageable, 61–70 developing, 51–60 bare minimum and at most 50 fail, subject to the domain-cut-off note. Dashboards are a strive/preference.

operative_change.summary: SOC efficacy scoring methodology and source anomaly.
operative_change.new_or_proposed_position: Use the signed report and five-domain weighted method, with zero denominators scored zero. evidence.supporting_text: Circular 24/113 dated August 20, 2024, addressed to 19 categories of 'All <RE type>' (AIFs, Bankers to an Issue/SCSBs, Clearing Corporations, CIS, CRAs, Custodians, DTs, Depositories, DDPs, DPs through Depositories, IAs/RAs, KRAs, MBs, MFs/AMCs, Portfolio Managers, RTAs, Stock Brokers through Exchanges, Stock Exchanges, VCFs). Background: SEBI issued a cybersecurity/cyber-resilience framework for MIIs in 2015, subsequently extended to Stock Brokers/DPs, MFs/AMCs, KRAs, QRTAs and Portfolio Managers; SEBI has also issued various cybersecurity-best-practice advisories to REs from time to time.

evidence.supporting_text: Paragraph 3: 'In order to strengthen the cybersecurity measures in Indian securities market, and to ensure adequate cyber resiliency against cybersecurity incidents/attacks, Cybersecurity and Cyber Resilience Framework (CSCRF) for SEBI REs has been formulated in consultation with the stakeholders... This framework shall supersede existing SEBI cybersecurity circulars/guidelines/advisories/letters (list of such superseded circulars/guidelines/advisories/letters are given as part of the framework attached as Annexure-1).' Paragraph 4 (Objective): CSCRF aims to address evolving cyber threats, align with industry standards, encourage efficient audits, ensure compliance, and sets standard reporting formats.
evidence.quote: This framework shall supersede existing SEBI cybersecurity circulars/ guidelines/ advisories/ letters
evidence.extraction_note: Bilingual page; right-half crop used.

evidence.supporting_text: Five cyber resiliency goals adopted from CERT-In's CCMP (Anticipate, Withstand, Contain, Recover, Evolve) mapped to six cybersecurity functions (Governance, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover); graded approach with five RE categories by span of operations/thresholds (MIIs, Qualified REs, Mid-size REs, Small-size REs, Self-certification REs); document structured into four Parts (I Objectives and Standards, II Guidelines, III Compliance Formats, IV Annexures and References); highlights governance/supply-chain risk management, data classification/localization, API security, SOC and measuring its efficacy, SBOM; CCI for MIIs/Qualified REs to monitor cyber-resilience progress periodically.
evidence.extraction_note: Bilingual page; right-half crop used.

evidence.supporting_text: 126 abbreviations defined (CCI, CSCRF, DR, MFA, RTO/RPO, SBOM, SOC, VAPT, etc.). Key definitions: Critical Systems (criteria for classification); Cyber Capability Index (CCI); Cyber Event/Cyber Resilience/Cyber Threat (FSB Cyber Lexicon); Cybersecurity Incident (CERT-In directions); Hosted Service (technical specifications including Tier-4 data-centre certification and a requirement that, if hosted outside India, a copy of REs' data in readable form be maintained within India); ISO 27001 certification; IT and Cybersecurity Data vs Regulatory Data; Major Change/Major Release (triggers mandatory VAPT); MIIs (Stock Exchanges, Depositories, Clearing Corporations, and per Box Item 1 also KRAs and QRTAs for CSCRF purposes); Principle of Least Privilege; Red team exercise; Regulated Entity; Regulatory Data (including the requirement that Regulatory Data be kept available, legible and usable within the legal boundaries of India); Risk (OWASP formula); Risk-based Authentication; Root Cause Analysis; SSDLC; SBOM; Trusted Channels.

evidence.locator: Section 1 Introduction, including Table 1 (List of SEBI cybersecurity circulars superseded) and Table 2 (List of SEBI cybersecurity letters/advisories superseded)
evidence.supporting_text: Introduction restates the five cyber-resiliency goals, six cybersecurity functions, and four-Part structure, and states: 'Cybersecurity and Cyber Resilience Framework (CSCRF) has been formulated to consolidate and strengthen the prevention, preparedness, and response capabilities against cyber-risks and cyber incidents.' Repeats the two-tier glide path (six categories with a pre-existing circular: January 1, 2025; others: April 1, 2025). Table 1 lists 21 circulars across 8 RE-category groupings (MIIs; Stock Brokers/DPs; MFs/AMCs; KRAs; QRTAs; Portfolio Managers; All REs; Stock Exchanges/CCs/Depositories) issued between July 6, 2015 and August 29, 2023, to be superseded by CSCRF. Table 2 lists 22 SEBI letters/advisories (to NSE, BSE, CDSL, ICCL, MCX, MCXCCL, MSEI, NCCL, NCDEX, NSE Clearing, NSDL, and AMFI) issued between October 30, 2019 and June 6, 2023 (mostly 'Submission of Cyber Audit Report' letters dated December 26, 2022, and 'Implementation of Cyber Capability Index' letters dated October 30, 2019), also to be superseded.
evidence.quote: Cybersecurity and Cyber Resilience Framework (CSCRF) has been formulated to consolidate and strengthen the prevention, preparedness, and response capabilities against cyber-risks and cyber incidents.
evidence.extraction_note: English-only single-column extraction; Table 1/Table 2 rows transcribed in full (see earlier_documents R001-R043).

evidence.supporting_text: Five broad categories (MIIs, Qualified REs, Mid-size REs, Small-size REs, Self-certification REs), decided annually based on prior-year data and fixed for the financial year. Entity-specific threshold tables for AIFs (AUM-based), Bankers to an Issue/SCSBs (RBI-guideline certificate), stock brokers (active-client-base/IBT-Algo-based), CIS and CRAs (Self-certification), Custodians (AUC-based), Debenture Trustees (largely Self-certification), Depository Participants (institutional/non-institutional), Designated Depository Participants (highest of DP/Custodian category), FPIs/FVCIs (excluded), Investment Advisers/Research Analysts (mostly excluded unless institutional), KRAs (treated at par with MIIs), LPCC (excluded), Merchant Bankers (conglomerate/issue-management-activity based), MFs/AMCs (AUM-based), Portfolio Managers (AUM-based), QDPs (excluded), REITs/InvITs (excluded), RTAs (folio-count-based; QRTAs are MIIs), Vault Managers (excluded), VCFs (corpus-based). Where an RE falls into more than one category, the highest applicable category governs.
evidence.extraction_note: English-only; multiple small threshold tables transcribed at a summary level.

evidence.supporting_text: Existing SCOT (MIIs) and Technology Committee (MFs/AMCs) must henceforth include one external independent cybersecurity expert. MIIs, Qualified REs and Mid-size REs must constitute an 'IT Committee for REs' with at least one external independent cybersecurity expert; for Small-size/Self-certification REs an IT Committee is not mandatory but compliance review defaults to MD/CEO/Board member/Partners/Proprietor. Brief Terms of Reference given (periodic review of cybersecurity policy implementation, incident reviews, deliberation on Board/SEBI-referred matters, compliance recommendations to the Board).
evidence.extraction_note: English-only extraction.

evidence.locator: Section 4 CSCRF Compliance, Audit Report Submission, and Timelines (Tables 15-23; paragraphs 4.1-4.5)
evidence.supporting_text: Table 15 sets applicability/periodicity for 16 standards (e.g., CCI third-party assessment half-yearly for MIIs / self-assessment annually for Qualified REs; policy review annually; IT Committee meetings quarterly; risk assessment half-yearly (MIIs)/annually (Qualified, Mid-size); privileged-user review quarterly/half-yearly; red-teaming and threat hunting half-yearly/quarterly for MIIs/Qualified REs). ISO 27001 certification mandatory for MIIs/Qualified REs within 1 year of CSCRF issuance (Table 16 sets reporting authority). VAPT: scope/periodicity (twice yearly for NCIIPC-protected systems, else once yearly) and timelines (report within 1 month of VAPT completion; findings closed within 3 months; revalidation within 5 months) (Tables 17-20). Cyber Audit: periodicity (twice yearly for MIIs/Qualified REs and IBT/Algo Mid-/Small-size REs; once yearly for the rest) and the same 1/3/5-month report/closure/follow-on timelines (Tables 21-23); Self-certification REs need only conduct VAPT (no other audit), submitting the Annexure-P self-certification. Market SOC must be set up mandatorily by NSE and BSE (optionally NSDL/CDSL) by January 1, 2025, with periodic efficacy reporting to SEBI.
evidence.extraction_note: English-only; multiple compliance tables transcribed at a summary level.

evidence.supporting_text: Mandates a CISO/Designated Officer (CISO for MIIs/Qualified REs, reporting directly to MD/CEO; Designated Officer for others); Board/Partners/Proprietor-approved cybersecurity and cyber-resilience policy encompassing CSCRF; cyber-risk management framework and risk register reviewed by the IT Committee for REs; CCI (23 parameters, Annexure-K) for MIIs/Qualified REs with a six-tier maturity rating (Exceptional 100-91 through Fail <=50); cybersecurity supply-chain risk management including SBOM for all new critical-system procurements (and within 6 months of CSCRF issuance for existing critical systems) and concentration-risk assessment/mitigation for third-party service providers.
evidence.extraction_note: English-only extraction.

evidence.supporting_text: Board/Partners/Proprietor-approved list of critical systems and comprehensive, time-bound asset inventory (including cloud assets, shared resources, data flows); periodic risk assessment including post-quantum risk; onboarding to the CERT-In intelligence platform; Box Item 7 on quantum-computing risk (cryptographic-asset inventory, PQC migration strategy, crypto-agility).
evidence.extraction_note: English-only extraction.

evidence.supporting_text: Access control (Principle of Least Privilege, Zero Trust, MFA for all critical-system access from untrusted to trusted networks), API security (rate-limiting, whitelisting), mobile-application security; cybersecurity awareness/training programmes; data-at-rest/in-transit/in-use encryption, data classification (Regulatory Data vs IT and Cybersecurity Data) with a data-localisation mandate (Regulatory Data kept accessible within India, with a carve-out for IT/Cybersecurity Data sent to global SOC/SaaS cybersecurity solutions, subject to annual Board/IT-Committee review); production/non-production environment separation; ISO 27001 certification and CIS Controls mandatory for MIIs/Qualified REs; patch-management timelines by criticality (High: 1 week; Moderate: 2 weeks; Low: 1 month).
evidence.extraction_note: English-only extraction.

evidence.supporting_text: SOC mandated 24x7x365 for all REs except client-based stock brokers with fewer than 100 clients, via own/group SOC, Market SOC, or third-party managed SOC; Market SOC mandatory for NSE and BSE (optional NSDL/CDSL), with Small-size/Self-certification REs mandated to onboard to Market SOC; SOC functional-efficacy measurement (Annexure-N) half-yearly for MIIs/Qualified REs; VAPT scope (Annexure-L); red-teaming exercises half-yearly and threat hunting quarterly for MIIs/Qualified REs.
evidence.extraction_note: English-only extraction.

evidence.supporting_text: Comprehensive Cyber Crisis Management Plan (CCMP) with scenario-based SOPs and an Incident Response Management Plan; four-tier incident classification (Low/Medium/High/Critical, detailed at Annexure-O); incidents falling under CERT-In directions reported to SEBI (via mkt_incidents@sebi.gov.in) and CERT-In within 6 hours, with details on the SEBI Incident Reporting Portal within 24 hours; Stock Brokers/DPs additionally report to Exchanges/Depositories within 6 hours; all other incidents reported to SEBI/CERT-In/NCIIPC within 24 hours; quarterly incident-summary reports to SEBI; Root Cause Analysis and forensic analysis as appropriate.
evidence.extraction_note: English-only extraction.

evidence.locator: Part I, Cybersecurity function: Recover (RC.RP/RC.CO/RC.IM) and Cyber Resilience Goal: Evolve (EV.ST)
evidence.supporting_text: On disruption of a critical system, RE must declare a 'Disaster' within 30 minutes; RTO of 2 hours (per IOSCO recommendation) and RPO of 15 minutes for all REs; scenario-based cyber-resilience testing at least twice yearly for MIIs/Qualified REs, with lessons shared with SEBI within 3 months; documented, Board/IT-Committee-approved backup and recovery plan (Annexure-C template) with off-site 'golden image' backups; Evolve strategies (threat modelling, heterogeneity, continuous adaptation) mandatory for MIIs/Qualified REs, periodic self-evaluation for Mid-/Small-size REs.
evidence.extraction_note: English-only extraction.

evidence.supporting_text: Self-certification and Small-size REs (Table 25, 46 standards) and Mid-size REs (Table 26, 9 standards) are exempted from a defined subset of standards, conditional on the RE being onboarded to Market SOC; Self-certification REs are additionally exempted from mandatory third-party cyber audit and periodic cybersecurity-posture evaluation, needing only VAPT.
evidence.extraction_note: English-only extraction; full exemption lists transcribed at a summary level (standard codes only, not individually itemised as separate legal_effects).

evidence.locator: Part II: CSCRF Guidelines (implementation guidance for every GV/ID/PR/DE/RS/RC/EV standard, tiered by RE-category applicability)
evidence.supporting_text: Detailed implementation guidance for each Part I standard, tiered by mandatory applicability across MIIs/Qualified/Mid-size/Small-size/Self-certification REs. Notable mandatory items beyond the Part I summary: CISO reporting line to MD/CEO for MIIs/Qualified REs; SBOM procurement timelines; concentration-risk controls for shared third-party providers; SEBI/government search-and-seizure and forensic-audit access rights over RE IT resources; mandatory zero-trust access for MIIs/Qualified REs; detailed mobile-application security controls (root/jailbreak detection, anti-tampering, re-authentication, no local storage of credentials); DNS/email security (SPF/DMARC/DKIM); Active Directory/Domain Controller hardening for MIIs; ISO 27001 certification scope (PDC, DR, NDR, SOC, co-location); auditor rotation (3-year maximum engagement, 2-year cooling-off); CCI self-/third-party assessment reporting within 15 days of completion; red-team lessons shared with SEBI within 3 months; CSK (Cyber Swachhta Kendra) onboarding for MIIs/Qualified REs; quarterly incident-summary reports to SEBI; RTO/RPO of 2 hours/15 minutes; immutable/air-gapped backups for ransomware resilience.
evidence.extraction_note: English-only extraction; this 54-page, highly granular technical-guideline section is summarised at the level of its distinctive mandatory obligations rather than reproduced guideline-by-guideline (see U001).

evidence.supporting_text: Annexure-A: standard VAPT reporting format including an authorised-signatory declaration, auditor's declaration/checklist, and a four-tier risk-rating scale (Critical/High/Medium/Low). Annexure-B: standard cyber-audit reporting format with an analogous declaration/checklist, a control-wise SEBI-CSCRF compliance-status table, and a standard exception-reporting format requiring IT-Committee approval of exceptions. Annexure-C: a reference recovery-plan template covering preparation, identification, containment, resolution and recovery checklists for a cybersecurity incident.

evidence.locator: Annexure-L (VAPT Scope), Annexure-M (Cyber-SOC Framework for MIIs reference), Annexure-N (Functional Efficacy of SOC)
evidence.supporting_text: Annexure-L: 10-item indicative VAPT scope (infrastructure/application VA, external PT, WiFi testing, API security testing, network segmentation, mobile VA/PT, OS/DB assessment, cloud VAPT, configuration audit) and testing-methodology standards (NCIIPC, CERT-In, NIST SP 800-115, ISO 27001, PCI-DSS, OSSTMM, OWASP). Annexure-M: cross-reference to SEBI's existing 'Cyber-SOC Framework for MIIs' circular (CIR/MRD/CSC/148/2018 dated December 7, 2018), which continues to govern the C-SOC requirement for MIIs. Annexure-N: five-domain SOC functional-efficacy scoring methodology (asset-technology coverage 25%, SOC operations 25%, personnel competency 20%, SOC governance 15%, SOC enrichments/enhancements 15%), each with its own detailed scoring tables.
evidence.extraction_note: English-only extraction; scoring-methodology tables summarised at domain level.

evidence.locator: Annexure-O: Classification and Handling of Cybersecurity Incidents (Tables 35-36)
evidence.supporting_text: Four-tier incident-severity classification (Low/Medium/High/Critical) with defined criteria (Table 35). Incident reporting: SEBI/CERT-In notification within 6 hours (via mkt_incidents@sebi.gov.in) and the SEBI Incident Reporting Portal within 24 hours; Stock Brokers/DPs additionally report to Exchanges/Depositories within 6 hours; non-CERT-In-direction incidents reported within 24 hours. Post-incident report-submission timelines (Table 36): Interim Report within 3 days, Mitigation-measure report within 7 days, Root Cause Analysis report within 30 days (extendable on request), Forensic Audit Report within a maximum of 75 days, VAPT-for-the-incident report within 45 days. Critical/High-severity incidents at MIIs, Qualified REs and Mid-size REs are mandatorily reviewed by the High-Powered Steering Committee on Cybersecurity (HPSC-CS); other severities are processed by SEBI internally. Non-reporting, deficient reporting, or non-implementation of HPSC-CS/SEBI recommendations within the prescribed timeline may attract appropriate regulatory action by SEBI.
evidence.extraction_note: English-only extraction.

evidence.locator: Annexure-P: Reporting Format for Self-certification REs
evidence.supporting_text: Standard self-certification reporting format for Self-certification REs: an authorised-signatory declaration confirming implementation/compliance with applicable CSCRF provisions, with the RE's VAPT report annexed.

evidence.extraction_note: Opening excerpt identifies the page; the substantive source-reviewed paraphrase is in each event-specific evidence entry.

evidence.supporting_text: Comply with CSCRF by January 1, 2025 for MIIs, stock brokers/DPs, mutual funds/AMCs, KRAs, QRTAs and portfolio managers already covered by cybersecurity circulars; other applicable REs have until April 1, 2025. The instruments in Tables 1–2 are deprecated according to that glide path. Table 2 also covers all April 19, 2023 letters with the stated mutual-fund/AMC/trustee advisory subject, rather than only the specimen letter number. These are compliance dates; August 20, 2024 is the issue date. The source establishes consolidation and replacement but does not establish a clause-by-clause historical difference for every control.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.supporting_text: Set the CSCRF category at the start of the financial year using the previous year’s data, retain it throughout that year and have it validated at compliance submission. Apply the highest category where multiple registrations exist. For CSCRF, the MII category includes KRAs and QRTAs. AIF AUM/VCF aggregate corpus thresholds are self below ₹100 crore, small ₹100–<500 crore, mid ₹500–<1,000 crore and qualified at least ₹1,000 crore. Brokers with up to 10,000 active UCC clients are self only without IBT/algo; with IBT/algo they are small; above 10,000–50,000 small, above 50,000–500,000 mid, above 500,000 qualified; QSB categorisation also applies. Custodian AUC is small below ₹1 lakh crore, mid ₹1–<10 lakh crore and qualified at least ₹10 lakh crore. Institutional DPs are qualified, other DPs mid; DDPs take the higher DP/custodian category. CIS, CRAs and non-excluded DTs are self; non-individual IAs small. Merchant bankers in conglomerate/systemically important groups are qualified, issue-management and the stated public-transaction activities mid, others small; listed merchant bankers also intimate exchanges. MF/AMC AUM is small below ₹10,000 crore, mid ₹10,000–<1 lakh crore, qualified at least ₹1 lakh crore. PMS is self below ₹1,000 crore, small ₹1,000–<3,000 crore, mid at least ₹3,000 crore. RTA folios are small 10,000–<1 crore, mid 1–<2 crore and QRTAs MII. Do not infer a QRTA threshold not stated here.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.locator: Section 2 exclusions and special arrangements; physical pages 39, 40, 41, 42, 43
evidence.supporting_text: Individual IAs, FPIs, FVCIs, LPCCs, REITs, InvITs, vault managers, RTAs below 10,000 folios and DTs with no new listed-debt issuer client in the preceding three financial years are excluded from CSCRF compliance submission as stated. QDPs are excluded from CSCRF compliance: preserve this different wording. RAs without another registration are excluded from submission but must provide the SaaS declaration under the November 3, 2020 advisory; an institutional RA with another registration follows that category. Bankers to an issue and SCSBs provide SEBI a certificate of compliance with RBI cybersecurity guidelines, and a listed bank also intimates its exchanges. Exclusion from submission must not be expanded into an unqualified exemption from every substantive requirement.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.supporting_text: Small/self Market-SOC users receive only these standard exemptions: GV.OC S1,S3; GV.RR S1,S4,S5; GV.OV S1–S4; GV.RM S1–S4; GV.SC S1,S2,S3,S6,S7; ID.AM S2,S6; ID.RA S1,S2,S3,S5; PR.AA S4,S15,S16,S17; PR.DS S1,S5,S6; PR.IP S3,S16,S17; PR.MA S1,S2; DE.CM S4; DE.DP S4,S5; RS.MA S2,S3,S5; EV.ST S1–S4. Self-certification REs additionally receive PR.IP S14 and EV.ST S5 exemptions. Mid-size Market-SOC users receive only GV.OV S4; ID.RA S3; PR.DS S5,S6; PR.IP S16,S17; DE.DP S4,S5; RS.MA S5 exemptions. Onboarding and category conditions travel with the affected controls; this is not a general exemption from cyber responsibility.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.supporting_text: Existing SCOT and mutual-fund technology committees add an independent external cybersecurity expert. Other MII, qualified and mid-size REs constitute an IT committee including such an expert. Small/self REs may constitute one; otherwise the MD/CEO/Board member/partner/proprietor performs review and approval. Additional terms cover policy, incidents and their impact/RCA, strengthening, referred matters and compliance; they supplement existing terms. Non-small/self committees meet quarterly and report recommendations/action to the Board. CII entities also follow the stated NCIIPC principles.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.locator: GV.OC S1–S3; GV.RR S1–S6; physical pages 53, 54, 55, 56, 79, 80, 81, 82
evidence.supporting_text: Identify organisational context, dependencies and legal requirements. Leadership establishes cyber roles, resources and accountability; obtain confidentiality/integrity agreements before access and provide role-appropriate training. MIIs/qualified REs appoint a CISO reporting directly to MD/CEO at least at CTO/CIO level, with capability and timely incident communication; other categories designate a senior officer. CII-specific roles follow NCIIPC. Comply with relevant SEBI and government cyber/data/IT laws and permit regulatory audits, inspection and IT-resource access including vendor resources. SEBI’s inspection/search/seizure powers are regulator powers, not instructions to REs to conduct seizures. Guideline budget and employment-program suggestions remain recommendations, subject to mandatory parent standards.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.supporting_text: Maintain an approved cyber/resilience policy, annual review, deviation reasons, updated risk policy and clear asset ownership, custody and approval chain. Mandatory guideline rows 1–5 include policy families, mobile/web financial-service policies and SEBI data access/vendor-contract responsibilities; the merged applicability cell extends through row 5. Rows beginning with the general identify/protect/detect/respond/recover and PDCA recommendations are not themselves universally mandatory guidelines. Apply the committee and CII-specific obligations in their stated cohorts.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.supporting_text: Review risk strategy and performance; integrate cybersecurity with enterprise risk, set appetite/tolerance, maintain a risk register and test scenarios with IT oversight. Risk assessments are half-yearly for MIIs and annual for qualified/mid-size REs. Consider assets, vendors, privacy, quantum threats, likelihood and impact and prioritise responses. Detailed non-small/self guidelines include ISO 27005 guidance, detection/response/containment metrics, fraud monitoring and Annex E scenarios. Quantum measures are indicative: inventories and priorities, migration strategy, skills/policy/proof of concept, exploration of PQC/QKD and crypto agility; the source does not mandate implementation of every example.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.locator: Definitions; GV.SC S1–S8 excluding separate SBOM event; Annex F/J references; physical pages 27, 28, 29, 60, 61, 85, 86, 87, 88, 89, 158, 162
evidence.supporting_text: Critical systems include core-impact and regulatory-data systems, connected devices, internet/client-facing and ancillary access/maintenance systems on premises or cloud. Maintain third-party identification, contracts, monitoring, joint recovery tests, concentration assessments and equal security standards. Hosted services require Tier-4-equivalent arrangements, cloud/audit equivalence, VAPT summaries, readable India copies where offshore, no kill switch and express contractual responsibility division. REs remain accountable for outsourced critical activities, background checks and NDAs. MIIs/qualified REs obtain vendor certifications where they lack control; MIIs remain responsible for NEAT/BOLT applications, not users. Non-small/self concentration reviews and exchanges’/depositories’ broker/DP vendor-concentration duties apply as stated. Annex F outsourcing and Annex J cloud circulars are referenced frameworks, not newly superseded instruments.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.locator: GV.SC S5 and SBOM guidelines; physical pages 60, 61, 86, 87, 88, 89
evidence.supporting_text: Obtain SBOMs for new critical software at procurement and keep updates. Obtain existing-system SBOMs within six months from CSCRF issuance. Include supplier, licence, dependencies, encryption, hash, updates, known/unknown components, access and error handling. Legacy/proprietary unavailability requires Board approval recording limitations, rationale and risk response. MII vendor-selection criteria apply additionally; the exception is not an automatic waiver.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.supporting_text: Maintain physical/digital/cloud/interface inventories, critical-system approval, data-flow/encryption maps, metadata and lifecycle control; prohibit unmanaged shadow IT. Update inventory/network architecture within three working days of change. MIIs maintain a configuration database; non-small/self REs use the stated IT service/lifecycle controls. The Market SOC exemption removes only the enumerated standard obligations.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.locator: ID.RA S3–S5 and guidelines; physical pages 59, 60, 89, 90, 91, 92
evidence.supporting_text: Onboard to CERT-In information channels, implement advisories within 24 hours of receipt or the time SEBI indicates, and monitor/report phishing domains to CSIRT/CERT-In. MII/qualified controls include dark-web monitoring, takedown/anti-phishing/rogue-app processes, indicators of attack/compromise and advisory SOPs; MIIs also use NCCC arrangements. Risk-sensitive authentication examples remain guidance. Conditional Market SOC exemptions apply to ID.RA S3.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.supporting_text: Maintain identity lifecycle, purpose/time/need-to-know access, least privilege, segregation, maker-checker, unique logs and physical/logical access policies; rank alone gives no access right. Revoke leavers/dormant/excess rights, lock failed logins and use MFA for untrusted access to trusted critical systems. Retain access logs at least two years, with six months online and the balance archived. Review access and privileged activity quarterly for MIIs/qualified and half-yearly for others. MII/qualified zero-trust and unused/delegated-token reviews are quarterly. Non-small/self requirements add privileged access management, password and internet controls, no alteration of own logs, network segmentation, web/email/DNS controls and allow-listing. All apply password complexity and deletion of unused generic IDs; more detailed password lifecycle/hash controls have the narrower applicability stated.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.locator: PR.AA broker isolation; Annex G expressly mandatory authentication; physical pages 93, 94, 95, 96, 159
evidence.supporting_text: A broker offering algorithmic trading isolates the algorithmic environment as specified. Internet-based trading and securities trading using wireless technology require at least two-factor authentication. Annex G’s surrounding passphrase, hashing, biometrics, reset, CAPTCHA and rate-limit examples are illustrative; they do not make every example a separate inflexible mandate. Preserve the underlying standards and equivalent-control audit requirement.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.supporting_text: Restrict physical access, accompany vendors, screen staff and immediately revoke departing staff access, protect critical rooms, control/log/audit remote support and supervise third parties. RDP is need-to-use with MFA, whitelisted IPs, fixed times and logs: clauses a–c continued onto page 99 apply to all REs. Only clause d environmental/service/access alerts is non-small/self. Maintain legal retention and disposal policies and appropriate secure wipe, degaussing, cryptographic shredding or destruction.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.supporting_text: Apply endpoint protection/detection, signatures and intrusion prevention; disable PowerShell/local administrator access by default except authorised use, review directory backdoors, test priority weaknesses and control removable media. MII domain controllers are patched on release with quarterly review, minimal software/administrators and no direct Internet access. Secure APIs with discovery, authentication, rate/throttle controls, OWASP risks and allow-lists; MIIs are responsible for their APIs consumed by REs. Mandatory mobile clauses a–l cover root/cloak/emulator safeguards, qualified exploration of jailbreak blocking, device/network checks, anti-malware/tamper/runtime signatures and published checksum, screen/voice warnings, reauthentication, sensitive-data/memory/SQL/encrypted-database controls. Device binding, MASVS and container-app clauses m–o share a nonmandatory cell. Generative-AI/open-source SOP guidance is also not labelled mandatory. Do not turn “explore” into unconditional implementation.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.locator: PR.AT S1–S5 and guidelines; physical pages 64, 103, 104, 105
evidence.supporting_text: Provide at least annual evolving cyber-awareness training and specific training for privileged users, third parties, executives/Board and physical/IT security roles. Run updated awareness/phishing exercises and extend to contractors where possible. Maintain technology-grievance forms, contacts and timelines and authenticated fraud reporting; optional written/authenticated requests and acknowledgement govern the described app access. Endeavour to provide seamless counterparty reporting and educate investors on phishing/credentials; do not promise an absolute seamless-reporting result.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.locator: PR.DS S1–S3; data localisation exception; physical pages 28, 29, 64, 65, 105, 106, 107
evidence.supporting_text: Keep regulatory data, including core/ancillary, investor communications and required/sensitive data, readable, usable and accessible in India. IT/cybersecurity data must exclude regulatory/sensitive data and must not regenerate it. Foreign global SOC/SaaS cyber processing is permitted for the defined IT/cyber data with annual IT-committee classification/assessment/review and Board approval. Supply requested data to SEBI/CERT-In/government within 48 hours. The exception does not allow regulatory data to be treated as cyber telemetry. Apply confidentiality, authorised storage, device and cloud controls in the stated cohorts.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.supporting_text: Protect data at rest/transit, classify it, maintain availability and leak controls, separate production and nonproduction and preserve integrity. Non-small/self guidelines require encryption including cloud in-use controls and full-disk/file encryption where possible. Customer-app security and real-time capacity planning apply except self. All protect backups/PII, avoid sensitive client-side HTML/cookie storage, renew certificates and use migration-integrity SOPs. MIIs/qualified REs separate environments and tests, address OWASP/SANS weaknesses and obtain critical source code or equivalent escrow including patches, vulnerability SLAs, vendor assessment and support. DevSecOps remains recommended. Annex H/I measures are illustrative except valid TLS expressly required for Internet pages with sensitive information; preserve equivalent-control audit requirements.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.supporting_text: Maintain approved baselines, secure development, change control, malicious-code scans, vendor certificates where source is not owned and security/functionality tests. All apply hardening, remove default accounts/services, restrict ports and scripting and use host firewalls where possible. Non-small/self guidelines require app allow-listing, regression before change, business-logic/security/load/recovery testing, vulnerability assessment at production releases and VAPT for major releases. A major release includes the specified regulatory, core software, login, interface, protocol, market and process/schema changes. Critical software receives DAST/SAST, cyber-functional/API and integrity audits, SOC logs, configuration audit, SBOM and a requirements matrix. New-technology maturity and threat-modelling examples remain guidance where labelled.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.locator: PR.IP S15; application-security certification; physical pages 66, 67, 112, 113, 114, 115
evidence.supporting_text: Apply critical application-security and functional-certification requirements according to software origin. Exchanges/depositories obtain STQC certification before COTS empanelment, maintain SOPs and obtain STQC/VAPT reports. Custom COTS items 1(a)–(d) and in-house items in paragraph 1 require the stated CERT-In auditor testing. SaaS/hosted applications meet technical specifications and all applicable CSCRF functions. Outsourcing does not remove RE accountability; do not impose exchange empanelment duties on every software user.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.supporting_text: Maintain and test backup/restore arrangements, physical/environment policies, SLA/protection effectiveness, response/recovery and vulnerability plans and the referenced cloud framework. Backup data and images offsite under IT-approved plans meeting recovery objectives. MII/qualified REs use offline encrypted backups and quarterly tests. Periodic external cyber-audit duties do not apply to the self-certification cohort. Annex C is a reference recovery-plan template including preparation, identification, containment, evidence, backups/golden images, resolution, invocation, teams, actions and lessons; its illustrative fields are not separate universally mandatory duties.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.supporting_text: Obtain the latest ISO 27001 certification within one year of CSCRF issuance, covering PDC, DR, NDR, SOC and co-location locations, and apply the stated recognised/CIS-equivalent security standards. Submit certification evidence with cyber audit to the exchange/depository for qualified brokers/DPs and SEBI for the other applicable entities. Certification is not required of every RE merely because it is addressed by the circular.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.supporting_text: Approve/log maintenance and remote access, assess vendor/remote risks and use severity-based OEM patches tested in an equivalent nonproduction environment before PDC/DR. Non-small/self remote-work controls include trusted devices, MAC/IP and host integrity and continuous alerts. Replace critical end-of-life/end-of-support systems; legacy virtual patching requires documented legitimate constraints and lasts at most six months. MIIs/qualified REs maintain an annually approved patch policy and quarterly compliance reports, test post-patch capacity and patch PDC/DR high severity within one week, moderate within two weeks and low within one month; emergencies follow the OEM clock.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.locator: Section 5; DE.CM S1; Market SOC guidelines; physical pages 51, 52, 68, 69, 115, 116, 117, 118, 119
evidence.supporting_text: NSE and BSE must establish Market SOC by January 1, 2025; NSDL and CDSL may do so. Small/self REs onboard subject to the client-based broker exception for fewer than 100 clients. Providers maintain minimum protocols, evolving controls, efficacy reports and annual activity audit and offer affordable VAPT/cyber-audit services for small/mid REs through CERT-In auditors. REs retain accountability. Market SOC participation grants only the express conditional exemptions.
evidence.extraction_note: Source-reviewed paraphrase. Locator lists the exact non-contiguous source pages; broad start/end range is not a claim that intervening pages impose the same requirement.

evidence.supporting_text: Operate continuous 24×7×365 monitoring across network, endpoints, physical/personnel and vendor resources, investigate alerts and monitor critical capacity. The SOC exception for brokers with fewer than 100 clients remains. MII/qualified SOC functional-efficacy review is half-yearly and includes the specified BAS/CART/decoy/vulnerability tools; managed/market users obtain annual provider efficacy reports. MIIs follow the separately referenced C-SOC circular in Annex M. Non-small/self detailed capacity duties cover storage, compute and bandwidth with proactive/reactive planning. Annex N assessment uses asset coverage 25%, operations 25%, personnel 20%, governance 15% and enhancement 15%; zero denominators score zero. Those scores are not ANS notification importance.

evidence.supporting_text: Use CERT-In-empanelled auditors for VAPT of all critical infrastructure, network/security, servers, databases, applications, LAN/WAN/public IP and web resources, including precommissioning and connected critical systems.
